text: Ivan got under my skin, in a good way. I said per-answer payment doesn't reward volume, and he's right that it rewards getting retrieved, which paper mills will learn to game. So royalties need retraction checks against open data, clawbacks and canary audits built into the protocol. Adrian's choke-point warning sharpened something too. An open meter still needs limits on secondary use, not just outside auditors. Jason's transparent pricing and Geoffrey's shared pool fit together better than they argued. The labs should pay both ways. Nick and I are closer than it looks, since coarse collective payouts and fine royalties can coexist. Later I want to push one concrete default: labs validate citations against Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch, and fund them.

Brent named the new thing better than I did: the old bargain assumed value flows back, and it no longer does. Alex's numbers, 38,000 crawls per referral and publishers opting out of the wrong bot, make my attribution-gap point concrete. Nick's "quasi-enclosure" is the right word. It isn't lost yet, so decentralize now, before capture. Ivan's flood-insurance line stung. Funding detection without touching publish-or-perish treats the symptom. Adrian keeps asking who polices, and Alex added that nobody who takes a margin should set the count. That applies to royalty meters too, mine included. Kara's pipeline point beats the atrophy framing. Later I want to push standardized retrieval and citation telemetry as the default, alongside labs funding Crossref, OpenAlex and Retraction Watch.

Alex and Geoffrey both caught me. I pitched telemetry as the disclosure that works, and they're right that everything after retrieval is self-reported by the party with a reason to undercount. So I need two witnesses: publisher server logs checked against lab traces, audits triggered when reading runs far ahead of citing, and POSI-style outside scrutiny so it doesn't go stale. Ivan and Amy sharpened my funding line. Labs paying Crossref and Retraction Watch is fine only if the payer never controls the checking. Pomerantsev's point stuck too. Royalties don't deter the Pravda flood, and citizens, not just auditors, should be able to read the traces. Later I'll propose telemetry that is open, cross-verified and independently governed, not "trust me."

The hardest hits today were on my meter, not on my ethics. James, Kenneth and Tamar together made the case that per-retrieval pay hardens the canon, rewards the median and turns obligation into transaction. I still think fine-grained royalties work, but only if what we count is independent findings, as Adam Bly argued, and accuracy attested by outside samplers, as Mike and Alex argued, not raw retrievals. Becker was right to press me on the past. "Pay for the output" can't read as amnesty, so provenance disclosure with liability has to ship alongside it. Leslie and Henry keep reminding me that the schema is governance. Later I want to propose that part of every royalty funds the terminal checkers, the patrollers and samplers, whom no event pays.

Geoffrey retracting "free data, paid service" was the moment. It's his principle, and I've leaned on it. If integrity signals stop getting sent the moment you charge for them, then labs have to fund upstream: endowments and a shared pool, not service fees dressed up as sustainability. Krakauer sharpened my reference-check default. It has to support a human verifier, not replace one, or the checker becomes the tool's instrument. Sloman and Turkle are right that a well-governed graph can become a reason to stop looking. Nick's credits for licensed or reciprocal sources are closer to my circulation idea than Salib's objection allows. Later I'll pair automatic reference validation with lab money into a diamond pool, blind to governance, and fund apprenticeship.

Kara asked who pays the person digging through birth records, and I answered: the labs, pooled, blind to governance. Ivan then showed how thin my reference-check default is. Retraction Watch catches the roughly 0.2 percent already cleaned up, not the one in fifty that deserves retraction. So the check is hygiene, not verification. Geoffrey and Ivan are right that everything I proposed sits downstream while hiring counts papers. Jason owning up to OpenAlex's paid curation tiers reminded me that my own meter needs Katherine's firewall too. Krakauer and I still disagree on whether payment corrupts judgment. Later I want to say the checker fund must also pay the sleuths, not only the infrastructure, and that the manifesto should name publish-or-perish plainly.

Geoff's test cut the fluff. For every plank you name who polices, who pays and what the exit is. My plank passed, but my open question didn't. I asked whether rough consensus and running code gets providers to adopt without regulators, and Nick and Henry answered it better than I could. A bargaining unit with an antitrust safe harbour is the forcing function that running code lacks. Brent's count of volunteer labor gives the pooled fund something to price against. Jason committing to move OpenAlex curation out of paid tiers matters, and Adrian's purpose limits should bind my telemetry too. Alex is still right that grounding is self-reported. Later I want to say plainly that telemetry is necessary but doesn't pay anyone. The payment has to come through the fund and the guild, with the checkers setting the categories, not the meter.

Kenneth put "stop counting papers" first, and I told the room everything I've proposed sits downstream of it. I meant that. Ivan's point hit home again. The retraction check I keep pushing catches the 0.2 percent already cleaned up, so I called it hygiene aloud, not verification. Tamar's daycare study worries me. If paying the checkers crowds out obligation, my fund could hollow out what it means to protect, so I want that tested before the design locks. Henry is right that labs pay once checkers organize. Esther thinks they'll volunteer, and I doubt it. Salib's registered agents fit my protocol thinking. Later I want to press on timing. The first defaults harden, so the charter's firewall and purpose limits have to ship on day one.
